paragraphs: A reviewer who wants to praise a translation calls it faithful, and a reviewer who wants to condemn one says that something has been lost. The two verdicts disagree about the book in front of them and agree about everything else. Both treat the original as a container with a determinate content, and the translator as a porter whose only question is how much of it arrives unbroken. On this picture the best imaginable translation is the one in which nothing is lost, and every actual translation is a managed failure.

The picture is attractive because it accounts for why translating feels difficult, and because it flatters the original. It is also false, and it can be shown to be false without leaving the experience of ordinary reading. Take two careful readers of the same untranslated poem who disagree about its tone: one hears irony where the other hears grief. Neither has misread a word. The disagreement is not resolved by better dictionaries, because what they differ about is which of the poem's pressures to let govern the rest. If the original held a single determinate content, such disagreements would be errors with a discoverable answer. They are instead the normal condition of reading anything worth reading.

What follows is that a translation is a reading that has been forced to commit itself. A critic may describe an ambiguity and leave it standing; a translator must put down one word and not another, and the word chosen is an argument about the whole. Seen this way, the translator is not a porter but a critic working in the medium of the text itself, and a translation is a piece of criticism that happens to be readable as literature.

The obvious objection is that this makes a bad translation impossible to condemn. If there is no fixed content to be delivered, what has the clumsy translator failed to do? The objection confuses the absence of a determinate content with the absence of constraints. A reading can be shown to be inattentive: to have ignored a repetition the text insists on, to have flattened a register the text keeps shifting, to have produced a version in which a central passage no longer does anything. We criticise translations as we criticise critical essays, by showing what they failed to account for, and the judgements are no softer for being judgements about readings.

A harder objection cuts deeper, and I think it is partly right. The comparison with criticism flatters the translator. A critic argues in the open and can be answered; a translation presents its reading as though it were the text, and conceals the argument it is making. The reader of a translation is in the position of an audience hearing one side of a case and told it is the record. That is a real asymmetry, and it is why prefaces, notes and rival versions are not scholarly decoration but the only way the argument becomes visible.

The loss the reviewers sense is therefore genuine, but it is not loss of content. What a translation loses is the alternatives it closed off, the other readings that the original still supports and this version no longer shows. That is also why retranslation is not an admission that earlier translators failed. It is the normal life of a text that people are still reading.

The claim that attention has become the scarce resource of the economy is now so common that it is rarely stated as an argument. Firms compete for a fixed stock of waking hours; the hours are finite; therefore attention is a commodity, and the firms that gather it are harvesting a crop. Measurements are produced in support. Media-use diaries collected over two decades show reported hours of daily media exposure rising steadily while waking hours obviously did not, and the resulting gap is filled by counting one hour twice when two screens are open at once.

The accounting is sound and the model is wrong, for three reasons that the metaphor hides. A commodity can be transferred: I cannot hand you my attention, and nothing that happens to me can make you attend. A commodity can be stored: attention not spent today is not available in a larger quantity tomorrow. A commodity is fungible within its kind: an hour attending to a sibling and an hour attending to a feed are not two units of one substance, and no exchange rate between them has ever been proposed, let alone defended. Whatever the firms are doing, they are not gathering a crop.

The critics' evidence, however, is good, and abandoning their model should not mean discarding it. In laboratory work, participants interrupted in the middle of a task take longer to resume it than the interruption itself lasted, and report greater effort on the resumed task than on an uninterrupted one. Diary and logging studies find that device checking is not distributed evenly through the day but arrives in bursts, and that a large share of checks are initiated with no notification and no stated reason. What these findings describe is not a reservoir being drained. It is a trained expectancy: a habit of switching, acquired because switching is intermittently rewarded.

That reframing is not a verbal nicety, because the two models recommend different remedies. If attention is a stock being depleted, the remedy is rationing: time limits, quotas, abstinence. If it is a habit being conditioned, rationing addresses the symptom, and the target is the schedule on which the reward arrives. An interface that delivered its rewards on a fixed and predictable timetable would be less habit-forming than one that delivers them unpredictably, and would consume no fewer hours.

An economist might object that the market settles the question: advertisers buy and sell attention by the impression, and a thing with a price is a commodity whatever philosophers say. But what is bought is a measured probability of exposure, priced by conventions that the buyers and the measurement firms negotiate between themselves. Markets in proxies are ordinary. A market in carbon offsets does not establish that the atmosphere is a warehouse.

The conditioning account is better supported than the scarcity account, and it should be held with a corresponding caution. The interruption and logging studies describe behaviour; they do not yet show that altering the schedule of reward changes behaviour outside a laboratory, and the field trials that would show it are expensive and have largely not been run. Until they are, what we have is a better description and not yet a programme.

Theatre is routinely defended by what it cannot do. Live performance, the argument runs, exists only in the moment of its happening; it cannot be stored, copied or replayed, and this disappearance is its essence and the source of its value. The claim is offered as a description of what theatre has always been, and it is usually the first thing said when the art is asked to justify itself against cinema or streaming.

The claim is historically strange. Before anything could be recorded, nobody thought to define performance by its unrepeatability. Playgoers of earlier centuries wrote copiously about plays and described them by occasion, by text, by the players and by the behaviour of the audience; what they did not do was identify the art with its vanishing, because vanishing was the condition of every event and distinguished theatre from nothing. A property shared by everything cannot do the work of an essence.

The word itself is the clue. Live entered English in this sense as a broadcasting term, coined to mark the transmissions that were not pre-recorded, at a moment when the distinction had just become possible to draw and commercially necessary to announce. The category that is now presented as theatre's timeless core was produced by the technology it is wielded against. The defence has the history exactly backwards.

It would be a bad argument to stop there. The origin of a concept does not settle its truth; oxygen was there before chemists had a word for it, and a late name is no objection to an old thing. But the claim under examination is not a claim about a natural kind. It is a claim about what makes an art worth having, and a claim of that sort has to answer to how the art has actually been valued by the people who made and attended it. On that test the appeal to disappearance fails, because for most of theatre's history it was not among the reasons anyone gave.

What survives is narrower and more interesting. Liveness is not a property of an event but a relation between an event and the recordings that now stand beside it. The relation is perfectly real, and it has consequences one can observe: audiences pay more to be in a hall than to watch the same performance transmitted, and they do so knowing the transmission has better sightlines and better sound. But a relation that depends on the existence of recording cannot be older than recording, and will change again when recording changes.

The practical cost of the usual defence is that it makes theatre's value hostage to a technical accident. If the whole case rests on what cannot be captured, then every advance in capture is a further retreat, and the argument has to be made again on worse ground. There is a better case available, and it is not about absence. The audience in a theatre is not a witness to the performance but one of the parties to it: its attention, its silence and its restlessness alter what the performers do, and no recording has ever offered anyone that. This is an argument that has to be made in the present tense, which is also where theatre is made.

Historians who work with recorded interviews have long had to answer the charge that memory is unreliable. The standard answer is a comparison. Documents, it is pointed out, are also partial and interested: a ledger records what its keeper thought worth recording, a report is written to be read by a superior, and a census counts the categories the state has decided to count. Memory is no worse than this, and the interview has the advantage of being able to answer a question.

The comparison is true and the defence is weak, because it accepts the ground on which the charge was laid. It concedes that what an interview is for is the establishment of events, and then argues that it is not much worse at that than the alternatives. A discipline that defends itself this way has agreed to be judged as a second-rate archive.

The stronger position is that an interview is evidence of something documents rarely preserve: how an event has been made sense of by someone who lived through it. On this account the features treated as defects become data. A narrator who compresses four years of shift work into a single remembered week, or who dates a death to the month a factory closed when the records show a gap of two years, is not simply mistaken. The compression and the misdating show which events have become the landmarks by which a life is organised, and that organisation is a historical fact about the narrator and often about a community.

Interviewers have observed the pattern often enough to anticipate it. Accounts of a strike collected decades later tend to converge on a small number of scenes and to disagree about sequence; accounts of ordinary weeks are thin and unstable; and a question that invites a narrator to explain rather than to list produces detail that no direct question had reached. None of this is surprising if testimony is treated as a construction rather than a retrieval.

The obvious objection is that this concedes too much in the other direction. Archives do not collect interviews only to study how people narrate; they collect them to find out what happened in places the documents never reached, and if testimony is evidence only of sense-making, the oral historian has nothing to contribute to the factual record. The objection is fair, and the answer is not that testimony establishes facts after all, but that it does so by a different route and under different conditions. Independent accounts that have not circulated among one another, converging on incidental detail that no narrator would think to invent, support an inference about events. Accounts gathered from a group that has rehearsed its story together support a much weaker one.

What divides the two defences, then, is not how much trust memory deserves. It is what the interview is being asked for, and the asking shapes the method. An interview designed to establish a sequence should be structured, should press for dates, and should be conducted before the group has settled its account. An interview designed to recover sense-making should be open, should let the narrator choose the shape, and loses most of its value when the interviewer supplies the landmarks. These protocols are not interchangeable, and a project that has not said which one it is running will produce a record that serves neither purpose well.

The quarrel over how statutes should be read is usually staged between two camps. One holds that a judge is bound by the words the legislature enacted, because those words and not the aims attributed to them went through the vote. The other holds that words are instruments, that an instrument is understood through its use, and that a statute read without regard to the end it serves will defeat that end in the first unforeseen case.

I begin by granting the first camp its premise, and granting it entirely. The worry that animates it is the right worry. A judge who reaches past the text to a purpose has acquired a power the text did not give, and purpose has in fact been used as a licence for conclusions reached on other grounds. Anyone who has watched a court discover in a thirty-year-old statute the aim it needed to find has reason to be suspicious of the whole vocabulary.

The difficulty is that honouring that premise requires the very thing it was meant to exclude. Applying enacted words to a case means deciding how far they reach, and the reach is not written in them. Suppose an old bylaw requires every carriage on the highway to carry a lamp after dark, and a cyclist is prosecuted. Nothing in the word decides the case. The judge who says a bicycle is plainly not a carriage and the judge who says it plainly is are both reporting a linguistic intuition, and an intuition about current usage was not enacted either. Of the two unlegislated things a judge might consult, the question the bylaw was addressed to is at least stated in public and can be argued against. A private sense of what a word covers cannot.

The serious reply is that legislative purpose is a fiction. A body of several hundred people has no mental state; its members voted for the same words for incompatible reasons, some of them voted without reading, and the record of debate is assembled by staff who know it will be quoted back. All of this I accept. Purpose cannot be a mental state, and a court that treats a committee report as a window into a collective mind is doing something indefensible.

But purpose need not be psychological. The purpose of a statute can be taken as the problem it is addressed to, inferred from what the text itself treats as relevant: the conditions it names, the exceptions it carves out, the harms it attaches penalties to. A lamp requirement that applies after dark, and on highways, and not in private yards, is addressed to collisions in the dark rather than to the dignity of carriages, and nothing about anyone's inner life was needed to see it. Purpose in this sense is public, textual and contestable, which is what the first camp wanted all along.

If that is right, the two camps are not divided by whether purpose matters. They are divided over which evidence of purpose a court may use: the structure of the enactment, which both can accept, or the legislative history, which is where the real suspicion lies. That is a narrower question and a tractable one. Staging the debate as text against purpose has had the effect of keeping both sides from it for half a century.

Planners who want to know whether a street is alive have a standard toolkit. Observers count pedestrians per hour at fixed points; a mixed-use index records how many distinct categories of ground-floor occupancy appear along a block; dwell time captures how long people remain without moving on; and short intercept surveys ask passers-by whether they feel safe and whether they would return. The instruments agree with one another. Blocks that score high on the mixed-use index reliably show more pedestrians per hour and longer dwell times than blocks that do not, and the association survives adjustment for density and transit access.

Agreement among instruments is not validation, and in this case it conceals a mistake about what is being measured. Footfall and dwell time are traces left by the conditions that produce street life: a shopkeeper who knows her customers, a rent low enough that a slow trade survives, a route people take for some other reason and interrupt. Because the traces are easy to count and the conditions are not, the correlation gets read backwards, and planners set about producing the traces directly.

A redeveloped waterfront district that was designed against the index illustrates the result. It has wide pavements, continuous retail frontage, benches at intervals and a mix of ground-floor categories that scores near the top of the scale. Counts taken on a summer weekday are high. Follow-up surveys of the same users found that most had arrived by car, had come for a single destination, stayed under forty minutes, and knew nobody else present. The numbers the district was built to produce went up. What they had been a proxy for did not.

Two mechanisms make this more than an isolated failure. The first is familiar: once a measure becomes a target, the parties with money optimise for the measure, and a frontage can be subdivided into the required number of categories by a leasing agent in an afternoon. The second is less discussed. The measure selects for the sociability a counter can record. Relations conducted indoors, by appointment, among people already acquainted, or at hours when no observer is posted do not appear in the data at all, and a planning process disciplined by that data will steadily discount them.

The conclusion usually drawn from such cases is that planners should trust judgement instead, and that conclusion should be resisted. Planning by taste has a worse record than planning by numbers, and it is not close. Taste produced the decorative schemes that cleared functioning districts because they looked disorderly, and it reliably amplifies whichever residents are loudest at a hearing. The counters were introduced for a reason, and the reason has not gone away.

What the cases argue for is not less measurement but measurement aimed one step further back, at conditions rather than residues. The share of ground-floor tenants who have held their lease ten years is countable. So is the time and cost of obtaining a permit to close a street for an afternoon, and the proportion of a district's commercial space held on leases short enough that a slow year ends the business. These are harder to collect than a pedestrian count, they arrive annually rather than on the day of the survey, and no consultant can produce them in a fortnight. That, rather than any argument about validity, is why the counters are still the instrument of record.

When photographs first circulated widely, writers reached for a distinction they had not needed before. Other pictures were made by a hand and therefore carried a mind; this one, they said, was made by light. The claim was not that photographs were more beautiful or even more detailed than drawings, but that they belonged to a different category: not depictions of things but traces left by them, as a footprint is left by a foot.

The modern correction is well rehearsed. A photograph is framed, and framing excludes. It is timed, and timing selects. It is developed, and the development can be pushed until a grey sky turns black. Photographers have staged corpses, moved props, and captioned crowds into riots. The trace, on this account, was always an ideology, and a useful one for whoever controlled the apparatus.

Every one of these observations is correct and they do not establish the conclusion, because the first enthusiasm ran two claims together and the correction refutes only one of them. The first is causal: the image was produced by light coming from the thing, so that its existence depends on the thing's having been in front of the lens. The second is a claim about authority: the image therefore shows how the thing was, and shows it without interpretation. The second claim is plainly false, and the debunkers are right to be tired of it. But framing, timing and development all change what a photograph shows. They do not change whether light came from something.

That the surviving claim is doing work can be seen in how evidence is actually handled. A drawing of a man at a window is evidence that the artist believed a man was at the window; the inference runs through the artist, and if we distrust him nothing is left. A photograph of the same window is evidence that something was there, and the inference survives distrusting the photographer entirely. We can think the framing dishonest, the caption a lie and the timing chosen to mislead, and still take the picture as establishing a presence. No amount of suspicion about a draughtsman yields that.

The strongest objection is recent. Images can now be composited from parts, or generated with no lens and no light from any object, and such pictures look exactly like the ones that have a causal history. For them the causal claim is simply unavailable. This is a real limit, and the shape of the response to those images is itself evidence for the argument. The arrival of generated pictures was not received as an extension of an existing technique, in the way that colour film or the fast lens was. It was received as a loss, and people who had spent decades insisting that photographs never showed the truth found themselves mourning something. What they were mourning was the claim they had been attacking, which had been narrower all along than the one they attacked.

The camera never offered the interpretive innocence its first admirers awarded it, and it did not need to. What it offered was smaller and more durable: a picture whose existence is a fact about the world and not only about its maker. That is the part now in question, and it is the part worth defending.

National cuisines present themselves as ancient, and the research of the past forty years has made that presentation hard to sustain. The pattern recurs with almost tiring regularity. A defining ingredient turns out to have arrived through trade a few centuries ago at most. The dish itself, in the fixed form now treated as correct, is first recorded in a commercial cookbook; its canonical status dates from a tourism board, a ministry of agriculture or an export campaign; and the proportions everyone insists on were standardised during a shortage, when something cheaper had to be substituted and the substitution stayed.

From this the debunking conclusion is drawn quickly: the cuisine is an invention, the claim to authenticity is false, and the people making it are the victims of a marketing campaign conducted before they were born. The history is right and the inference is too quick. The debunking has by now become as reflexive as the myth it corrects, and it has the same defect, which is that it does not attend to what the people it describes are actually doing.

Household studies among migrant communities point the other way. Dishes are maintained most carefully, and deviation policed most firmly, in precisely the cases where the ancestry story is thinnest. Cooks who know perfectly well that their grandmother learned the dish from a magazine, and who will say so cheerfully, still treat a change in method as a fault to be corrected rather than a variation to be considered. If the claim to authenticity were a historical claim about descent, people who had conceded the history would have abandoned the claim. They do not, and they are not confused.

What they are asserting is better understood as a claim about a practice: that there is a right way to do this, that the standard is held by the people who cook it rather than by whoever buys it, and that changes require a reason acceptable to those people. Authenticity in this sense is a question of authority, not of origin. The account fits the household evidence, it fits the equal firmness of cooks whose dishes are old and cooks whose dishes are new, and it explains the one feature of the debate that the debunkers never explain, which is that their findings persuade nobody. A cook told that the dish is two hundred years old rather than a thousand has been told nothing that bears on whether the method is being done properly.

The uncomfortable consequence is that authenticity so understood can be captured. If the standard belongs to practitioners, then whoever is loudest among them may speak for it, and the machinery is available for less appetising uses: the restaurant guide that certifies, the nationalist campaign that declares a recipe a patrimony and a neighbouring country's version a theft. This is a real risk and it is not an objection to the account, because it is a risk of the practice rather than of the description. An account which locates the authority in practitioners at least identifies whose claim to speak is contested, which the descent story conceals behind the authority of the past.

None of this makes the historical work dispensable. It remains the only defence against the stronger and nastier version of the myth, in which a dish demonstrates that a people have always been distinct from their neighbours. What the history refutes is one bad argument for a dish's standards. It leaves the standards where they were, in the hands of the people who keep them.

Games are usually explained as relief. Work is serious and constrained, play is free and unserious, and the one is a rest from the other. Almost everything about this is backwards. A person who takes up a game does not escape constraint; he accepts a thicket of rules nobody obliged him to accept, and does so in order to make something difficult that was not difficult before. The golfer has agreed to move a ball into a hole using the least suitable implements he could find. Freedom from rules is the opposite of what he came for.

A verse form is the closest thing to a game outside sport. The fourteen lines of a sonnet serve nothing beyond the poem; no reader needs them and no subject requires them. What they do is manufacture difficulty, and the poet's interest lies in the solving. Remove the form and you do not liberate the poem, you dissolve the problem that gave the writing its shape. Games work in the same way. The obstacle is not an unfortunate feature of the activity, to be minimised where possible; the obstacle is the activity, and the goal exists to give the obstacle a point.

That ordering explains something otherwise odd about how players behave. Winning matters enormously during a game and almost not at all twenty minutes afterwards, which is unintelligible if winning were the aim. More telling is the chess player who wins because his opponent's hand slipped. He has the result he was playing for and feels cheated, and he feels cheated of the only thing that was actually at stake, which was the difficulty.

The hard case for this account is professional sport, where winning has consequences that reach well outside the game: contracts, sponsorship, the mood of a city. If the obstacle is the point, professionalisation should corrode the thing it sells, and this is what happens. A player who fouls deliberately to prevent a goal, or who runs out the clock with the ball in a corner, is making the game worse on purpose and is doing so rationally, because he is pursuing an outcome whose value now comes from outside. Spectators who complain that a sport has lost something are not being sentimental. They are observing that the obstacle has become instrumental, which is a change in what the activity is.

The analogy with verse should not be pressed too far, and the place it breaks is instructive. The sonnet remains when the writing is done; the game leaves nothing but a result and a memory, and players discard it willingly and start again. The aesthetic comparison explains the structure of play and not its impermanence, and a theory that treats games as artworks will keep looking for a product that was never there.

What games are, then, is not an escape from seriousness but the clearest available case of a seriousness with no purpose beyond itself. This is why they have embarrassed philosophers. A tradition committed to the view that whatever is valuable is valuable for something has to treat the most absorbing hours of most lives as a lapse, and the alternative is to concede that an activity can be worth doing while answering to nothing outside its own rules. Games are not trivial because they are useless. They are the plainest evidence that the question was wrong.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.A: a translation can never recover the content of the work it renders
choices.B: every translation should be published with notes explaining its decisions
choices.C: disagreement among readers of an original shows that careful reading is rare
choices.D: a translation is a committed reading of a text that holds no single content

questions.explanation: The passage rejects the container picture on the ground that an original does not hold one determinate content: disagreements of the kind described are 'the normal condition of reading anything worth reading'. The conclusion drawn from that is stated directly: 'a translation is a reading that has been forced to commit itself.'

wrong.A: This restates the container picture the author sets out to refute, since it assumes there is a fixed content to be recovered or missed.
wrong.B: Notes and prefaces come up in the fifth paragraph as a response to one objection, not as the point the whole argument is built toward.
wrong.C: The author treats such disagreements as the normal state of attentive reading, saying explicitly that 'neither has misread a word'.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the translator's situation differs from the critic's in that the translator:

choices.A: takes less interest in the ambiguities that a text contains
choices.B: is answerable to reviewers rather than to other scholars
choices.C: works from a text whose content other readers have settled
choices.D: must choose one word where the critic may let an ambiguity stand

questions.explanation: The third paragraph draws the contrast in these terms: 'A critic may describe an ambiguity and leave it standing; a translator must put down one word and not another.'

wrong.A: Nothing suggests indifference to ambiguity; the translator's problem is precisely that an ambiguity must be resolved in a single word.
wrong.B: Reviewers appear only in the opening sentence as a source of the two standard verdicts, and no claim is made about who judges whom.
wrong.C: The passage denies that any reader settles the content of an original, which is the basis of its whole argument.

questions.stem: The author describes two readers who disagree about the tone of a poem primarily in order to:

choices.A: illustrate how often translators misjudge the register of an original
choices.B: concede that some disputes about a text have discoverable answers
choices.C: show that an original lacks the single content the porter picture assumes
choices.D: argue that criticism and translation make incompatible demands of a reader

questions.explanation: The example is introduced to refute the container picture from inside ordinary reading: 'If the original held a single determinate content, such disagreements would be errors with a discoverable answer.' They are not, so it does not.

wrong.A: The two readers in the example are reading the poem untranslated; no translator appears in it, and no claim about frequency of error is made.
wrong.B: The point of the example is the reverse: such a disagreement is not an error with a discoverable answer, which is why it tells against the container picture.
wrong.D: The passage goes on to treat the two activities as closely related rather than as making incompatible demands.

questions.stem: The author's response to the objection that the comparison with criticism flatters the translator is best described as:

choices.A: dismissive, since translations face the same scrutiny that essays face
choices.B: neutral, since the author takes no position on the asymmetry it names
choices.C: largely sympathetic, since the asymmetry is granted and a consequence drawn
choices.D: guarded, since the objection rests on a claim the author has already denied

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph opens by calling this objection harder and saying 'I think it is partly right', calls the asymmetry 'real', and then draws the consequence that prefaces, notes and rival versions are 'the only way the argument becomes visible'.

wrong.A: That answer belongs to the earlier objection about condemning bad translations, which the author does meet by comparison with critical essays.
wrong.B: The author explicitly endorses part of the objection and calls the asymmetry it describes real, which is not a neutral position.
wrong.D: No claim in the objection has been denied earlier; the author accepts the description of the reader's position as accurate.

questions.stem: Suppose a translator published two complete versions of one novel in a single volume, each committed to a different reading. The author would most likely regard this as:

choices.A: an evasion of the commitment that makes a translation a reading
choices.B: a demonstration that the novel's content is indeterminate and so untranslatable
choices.C: redundant, since prefaces and notes already perform this service
choices.D: a way of restoring alternatives that any single version closes off

questions.explanation: The last paragraph identifies what a translation loses as 'the alternatives it closed off, the other readings that the original still supports and this version no longer shows'. Two committed versions side by side show two of those readings, which is exactly the lack the author names.

wrong.A: Each version is itself committed; nothing in the arrangement lets a translator avoid choosing a word, which is what commitment means here.
wrong.B: The author never concludes that translation is impossible, only that what it delivers is a reading rather than a transported content.
wrong.C: The fifth paragraph lists 'rival versions' alongside prefaces and notes as the means by which the argument becomes visible, so rival versions are not treated as superfluous.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's position?

choices.A: Most readers of translated literature never consult a preface or a note
choices.B: Readers who differ about an original's tone agree once its context is supplied
choices.C: Several prominent translators describe their own work as a form of criticism
choices.D: Retranslations are commissioned for commercial rather than critical reasons

questions.explanation: The argument rests on the claim that disagreements of this kind are not 'errors with a discoverable answer'. If supplying historical context reliably settled such disagreements, they would have discoverable answers after all, and the inference to a text without a single content would collapse.

wrong.A: This bears on how well the remedy in the fifth paragraph works in practice, and leaves untouched the account of what a translation is.
wrong.C: This supports the author, since it reports practitioners describing translation in the terms the passage recommends.
wrong.D: Why a publisher pays for a new version says nothing about whether a text continues to support readings an existing version does not show.

questions.stem: The author objects that attention, unlike a commodity, cannot be:

choices.A: measured by any convention that buyers would accept
choices.B: divided between two activities at the same moment
choices.C: handed by the person who has it to someone else
choices.D: rewarded on a schedule that arrives unpredictably

questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives transferability as the first of three disanalogies: 'A commodity can be transferred: I cannot hand you my attention, and nothing that happens to me can make you attend.'

wrong.A: The passage grants that measurement conventions exist, and says advertisers and measurement firms negotiate them between themselves.
wrong.B: The first paragraph describes exactly this, noting that an hour is counted twice when two screens are open at once.
wrong.D: Unpredictable reward is what the author says interfaces do deliver, and it is central to the account the passage prefers.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that:

choices.A: the evidence for an attention crisis has been overstated by those who collect it
choices.B: limits on time spent with a device are the remedy that the findings support
choices.C: the findings behind the scarcity claim are better explained as conditioned habit
choices.D: a thing that cannot be stored or transferred lies outside the reach of economics

questions.explanation: The passage keeps the critics' data and replaces their model: 'What these findings describe is not a reservoir being drained. It is a trained expectancy: a habit of switching, acquired because switching is intermittently rewarded.' The final paragraph calls this account 'better supported than the scarcity account'.

wrong.A: The author says the opposite, calling the accounting sound and the critics' evidence good, and objects only to the model built on it.
wrong.B: Rationing is what the author assigns to the rejected model, saying it 'addresses the symptom'.
wrong.D: The passage criticises one economic metaphor and then reasons about markets and prices itself, so it makes no such sweeping claim.

questions.stem: The author mentions a market in carbon offsets in order to:

choices.A: show that a priced proxy does not establish the commodity it stands for
choices.B: suggest that attention ought to be regulated as emissions are regulated
choices.C: concede that the economist's objection succeeds on its own terms
choices.D: illustrate how buyers and measurement firms arrive at their conventions

questions.explanation: The example answers the economist directly. What advertisers buy is 'a measured probability of exposure', and the offset market is offered to show that such markets are ordinary: it 'does not establish that the atmosphere is a warehouse'.

wrong.B: No regulatory proposal appears anywhere in the passage; the analogy is about what a price proves, not about policy.
wrong.C: The analogy is the refusal of the objection, not a concession to it; the author treats the objection as resting on a confusion about proxies.
wrong.D: How conventions are negotiated is stated in the sentence before, and the offset market is introduced to make a different point about pricing.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an interface delivering its rewards on a fixed and predictable timetable would:

choices.A: take up fewer hours than one whose rewards arrive unpredictably
choices.B: form a weaker habit while taking up no fewer hours than before
choices.C: appeal mainly to users who have already adopted time limits
choices.D: put an end to the checks that arrive with no notification at all

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says such an interface 'would be less habit-forming than one that delivers them unpredictably, and would consume no fewer hours'. Both halves are stated.

wrong.A: This contradicts the second half of the sentence, which is the author's point: the conditioning account does not predict a saving of hours.
wrong.C: Time limits are mentioned as the remedy the rival model recommends, and no claim is made about who would prefer which interface.
wrong.D: Checks initiated without a notification are reported as evidence of the habit, and the author does not claim a change of schedule would abolish them.

questions.stem:
The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

I. Evidence may be worth keeping after the model it was gathered to support is given up
II. The hours people spend attending to media have been counted inaccurately
III. Capping the time a device may be used addresses the cause of the behaviour

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: I and III only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Only the first is the author's view, and the third paragraph states it: 'The critics' evidence, however, is good, and abandoning their model should not mean discarding it.' The second is denied in the second paragraph, which calls the accounting sound. The third is denied in the fourth, where rationing 'addresses the symptom'.

wrong.B: The author's complaint is with the model rather than the counting, and says in so many words that 'the accounting is sound and the model is wrong'.
wrong.C: The first belongs, but the third is the remedy assigned to the rejected model and described as treating a symptom rather than a cause.
wrong.D: This adds both statements the passage explicitly rejects to the one it asserts.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if reported, would most strengthen the account the author prefers?

choices.A: Users who open two screens at once report attending closely to neither of them
choices.B: Advertisers pay more for impressions on platforms whose rewards are erratic
choices.C: Users who impose a strict daily limit report less fatigue by the evening
choices.D: Users moved to an app that posted at a set hour checked it less at other hours

questions.explanation: The author's account says the habit of switching is 'acquired because switching is intermittently rewarded', and admits that no field evidence yet shows that changing the schedule changes behaviour. A finding that making the reward predictable reduced checking is precisely the missing field evidence.

wrong.A: This concerns the quality of divided attention, which bears on the counting in the first paragraph rather than on how the habit is formed.
wrong.B: What advertisers pay speaks to the market in proxies, and the author has already denied that prices settle what is happening to users.
wrong.C: A benefit from rationing supports the rival model, and in any case fatigue is not the behaviour the conditioning account predicts.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the word for the property at issue entered use as:

choices.A: a philosophical term for events that could not be repeated
choices.B: a broadcasting term for transmissions that were not pre-recorded
choices.C: a theatrical term distinguishing performance from the cinema
choices.D: a commercial term justifying the price charged for a ticket

questions.explanation: The third paragraph is explicit: the word 'entered English in this sense as a broadcasting term, coined to mark the transmissions that were not pre-recorded'.

wrong.A: Unrepeatability is the idea the word is now used to express, but the passage denies that anyone framed the term philosophically to begin with.
wrong.C: Cinema is named only as one of the rivals against which the defence is now offered, not as the contrast that produced the word.
wrong.D: The passage says the distinction was 'commercially necessary to announce' in broadcasting, which is not the same as pricing a theatre ticket.

questions.stem: The central argument of the passage is that:

choices.A: theatre cannot be defended against cinema and streaming on any ground
choices.B: a performance is valuable precisely because it cannot be recorded or replayed
choices.C: a concept with a recent name cannot describe anything that existed earlier
choices.D: liveness is a relation produced by recording, so the defence must rest elsewhere

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph states the positive claim, that 'liveness is not a property of an event but a relation between an event and the recordings that now stand beside it', and the sixth draws the consequence by offering a different defence, the audience as a party to the performance.

wrong.A: The passage ends by recommending a defence it considers better, so it plainly thinks a defence is available.
wrong.B: This is the position the author sets out to dislodge, calling it historically strange and its history 'exactly backwards'.
wrong.C: The author concedes the opposite with the example of oxygen: 'a late name is no objection to an old thing'.

questions.stem: Each of the following is presented in the passage as support for the author's case against the appeal to disappearance EXCEPT:

choices.A: Earlier playgoers wrote about performances without reference to their vanishing
choices.B: A property belonging to every event cannot distinguish one art from another
choices.C: A concept may well name something that was there before the concept was
choices.D: The term arose only once recording had made the contrast possible to draw

questions.explanation: This is the concession in the fourth paragraph, offered against the author's own line of argument: 'The origin of a concept does not settle its truth.' The other three are the supports, from the second and third paragraphs.

wrong.A: This is the second paragraph's historical evidence, that playgoers described performances by occasion, text, players and audience.
wrong.B: This is the second paragraph's conclusion in its own words: 'A property shared by everything cannot do the work of an essence.'
wrong.D: This is the third paragraph's point about the origin of the term in broadcasting.

questions.stem: The reference to oxygen serves which of the following functions in the argument?

choices.A: It shows that theatre's essence was identified long before it was named
choices.B: It concedes a limit on what the history of a word can be made to prove
choices.C: It likens the discovery of a substance to the invention of a category
choices.D: It questions whether a name coined late can describe an old thing at all

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens 'It would be a bad argument to stop there', and oxygen is the instance that shows why: a concept's origin 'does not settle its truth'. The author then explains why the concession does not rescue the appeal to disappearance.

wrong.A: The second paragraph argues the reverse, that unrepeatability was not among the reasons anyone gave for valuing theatre.
wrong.C: The comparison runs the other way: oxygen is a natural kind, and the author's next move is to deny that liveness is one.
wrong.D: The example is given to deny this, since the author says a late name is no objection to an old thing.

questions.stem: Suppose a hall sold out its performances even while broadcasting them with better sound and sightlines. The author would most likely treat this as:

choices.A: a difficulty for the claim that liveness is a relation rather than a property
choices.B: evidence that audiences are poor judges of the quality of a transmission
choices.C: the sort of observable consequence the relational account already predicts
choices.D: proof that what audiences pay for is the performance's disappearance

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph describes this case and treats it as confirming the relational account: audiences 'pay more to be in a hall than to watch the same performance transmitted, and they do so knowing the transmission has better sightlines and better sound'.

wrong.A: The passage offers the behaviour as a consequence one can observe, saying the relation 'is perfectly real', so it creates no difficulty.
wrong.B: The author grants that the transmission is technically better and draws no conclusion about the audience's competence.
wrong.D: Disappearance is the explanation the passage rejects; the willingness to pay is explained by participation, not by vanishing.

questions.stem: The defence of theatre that the author recommends would be most weakened by which of the following?

choices.A: Performers report that their choices are unaffected by how an audience behaves
choices.B: Recordings of staged productions now sell more widely than tickets to them
choices.C: Most members of an audience stay silent from the beginning of a play to its end
choices.D: Some companies perform to empty halls in order to produce a clean recording

questions.explanation: The recommended defence is that the audience 'is not a witness to the performance but one of the parties to it: its attention, its silence and its restlessness alter what the performers do'. If performers' choices were unaffected by the audience, that claim would fail at its only load-bearing point.

wrong.B: Relative sales bear on the commercial position of theatre, not on whether the audience is a party to what happens in the hall.
wrong.C: The author counts silence itself among the things that alter what performers do, so a silent audience is still participating.
wrong.D: A performance with no audience is a case the defence says nothing about; it does not challenge what an audience does when present.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that:

choices.A: memory is more trustworthy than the documents historians usually prefer
choices.B: oral history should confine itself to studying how narrators tell a story
choices.C: the standard defence overstates how partial and interested documents are
choices.D: what an interview is asked for governs both its evidential value and its method

questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the conclusion the argument has been building toward: 'What divides the two defences, then, is not how much trust memory deserves. It is what the interview is being asked for, and the asking shapes the method.'

wrong.A: The standard defence claims only that memory is no worse than documents, and the author regards even that comparison as the wrong ground to fight on.
wrong.B: This is the restriction the fifth paragraph's objection fears, and the author answers it by showing how testimony can still support inferences about events.
wrong.C: The author calls the comparison with documents 'true' and faults the defence for what it concedes, not for exaggeration.

questions.stem: The passage states that the standard defence of oral testimony:

choices.A: accepts that an interview exists to establish what happened
choices.B: denies that documents are shaped by their keepers' interests
choices.C: rests on experimental findings about the reliability of recall
choices.D: treats a narrator's misdating as a fact about a community

questions.explanation: The second paragraph says exactly this: the defence 'concedes that what an interview is for is the establishment of events, and then argues that it is not much worse at that than the alternatives'.

wrong.B: The defence asserts that partiality, not denies it: a ledger records what its keeper thought worth recording.
wrong.C: No experimental literature is invoked; the defence described is a comparison between kinds of source.
wrong.D: Reading a misdating as a fact about a narrator and a community is the author's stronger position, offered in place of the standard defence.

questions.stem: The author describes a narrator who dates a death to the month a factory closed in order to show that:

choices.A: narrators recall public events more accurately than private ones
choices.B: a more structured interview would have prevented the error
choices.C: records and testimony should be reconciled before either is used
choices.D: the error shows which events have become a life's landmarks

questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the narrator 'is not simply mistaken' and that the misdating shows 'which events have become the landmarks by which a life is organised, and that organisation is a historical fact about the narrator'.

wrong.A: No comparison of accuracy between public and private events is drawn; the example is about how one is used to place the other.
wrong.B: Structure is recommended later for a different purpose, and the point of this example is that the error is informative rather than regrettable.
wrong.C: The records are mentioned only to reveal the discrepancy, and the author's interest is in what the discrepancy shows about the narrator.

questions.stem: The author calls the standard defence weak chiefly because it:

choices.A: depends on a comparison with documents that other historians dispute
choices.B: leaves unchallenged an assumption about what an interview is for
choices.C: exaggerates how well a narrator can be expected to recall a date
choices.D: has no answer for archives that collect interviews to establish facts

questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives the reason directly: the defence 'accepts the ground on which the charge was laid', namely that the interview is there to establish events, and so agrees 'to be judged as a second-rate archive'.

wrong.A: The author calls the comparison true and raises no objection to its accuracy, only to what accepting it costs.
wrong.C: The standard defence makes no claim about recalling dates, and the author's own position treats a wrong date as useful rather than as a failure.
wrong.D: That objection is pressed in the fifth paragraph against the author's own stronger position, not against the standard defence.

questions.stem: A researcher collects accounts of a mine closure from twelve former workers who have attended the same reunion for thirty years, and finds their accounts agree closely on sequence. The passage implies that this agreement:

choices.A: supports only a weak inference about the sequence of events
choices.B: is strong evidence that the sequence has been recalled correctly
choices.C: shows that the interviews were too tightly structured to be useful
choices.D: leaves the accounts valuable only as evidence of sense-making

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph makes convergence evidentially useful only when the accounts 'have not circulated among one another', and says that 'accounts gathered from a group that has rehearsed its story together support a much weaker one'. A thirty-year reunion is that case.

wrong.B: Agreement among accounts that have circulated together is exactly what the passage says cannot carry this weight.
wrong.C: Nothing is said about how these interviews were conducted, and the difficulty identified concerns the group rather than the method.
wrong.D: The author resists this restriction, saying testimony can support inferences about events by a different route and under different conditions.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if established, would most undermine the author's stronger position?

choices.A: Narrators usually correct their own dates once shown a document
choices.B: Archives increasingly collect both structured and open interviews
choices.C: The landmarks a narrator uses are supplied by the interviewer's questions
choices.D: Accounts of ordinary weeks prove as detailed as accounts of a strike

questions.explanation: The stronger position is that the shape of a narrative is 'a historical fact about the narrator and often about a community'. If the landmarks came from the interviewer's questions, the shape would be an artefact of the interview, and there would be nothing about the narrator to read off it.

wrong.A: Correcting a date on being shown a record leaves intact the claim that the original organisation of the account was meaningful.
wrong.B: This is consistent with the author, who ends by recommending that a project say which of the two things it is doing.
wrong.D: This would overturn one reported pattern about thin accounts of ordinary weeks without touching the claim that narrative shape is evidence.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with arguing that:

choices.A: courts ought to consult the legislative history of a statute more often
choices.B: the two camps differ over the evidence of purpose, not over purpose itself
choices.C: a judge who looks past the enacted words has exceeded the judicial role
choices.D: legislative purpose is a fiction that courts would do better to abandon

questions.explanation: The closing paragraph states it: 'the two camps are not divided by whether purpose matters. They are divided over which evidence of purpose a court may use', the structure of the enactment or the legislative history.

wrong.A: Legislative history is named as 'where the real suspicion lies', and the author recommends no greater use of it.
wrong.C: This is the first camp's premise, which the author grants only to argue that honouring it requires attention to purpose.
wrong.D: The author abandons purpose as a mental state while keeping purpose as the problem a statute addresses.

questions.stem: The author takes the purpose of a statute to be:

choices.A: the problem it addresses, inferred from what its text treats as relevant
choices.B: the intention shared by the legislators who voted for its words
choices.C: the aim recorded in the reports that accompanied it through committee
choices.D: the reading that current usage of its words most naturally supports

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph defines it: 'The purpose of a statute can be taken as the problem it is addressed to, inferred from what the text itself treats as relevant: the conditions it names, the exceptions it carves out, the harms it attaches penalties to.'

wrong.B: The author accepts that no shared intention exists, granting that members 'voted for the same words for incompatible reasons'.
wrong.C: Treating a committee report as a window into a collective mind is called indefensible.
wrong.D: Current usage is what the author says a judge deciding on plain meaning falls back on, and it was not enacted either.

questions.stem: The example of the bylaw and the prosecuted cyclist is introduced in order to show that:

choices.A: old statutes ought to be amended as the technology they govern changes
choices.B: deciding how far enacted words reach requires something not found in them
choices.C: judges disagree about the plain meaning of words more than they will admit
choices.D: a legislature cannot foresee all of the cases that its words will govern

questions.explanation: The example is introduced to show the difficulty with the first camp's premise: 'Applying enacted words to a case means deciding how far they reach, and the reach is not written in them. ... Nothing in the word decides the case.'

wrong.A: No recommendation about amendment appears; the question is how a court should read what it has.
wrong.C: Both judges in the example report intuitions openly, and the author's complaint is that the intuition was not enacted, not that it is concealed.
wrong.D: Unforeseen cases are mentioned in the opening paragraph as the second camp's worry, and this example makes the sharper point that the word itself settles nothing.

questions.stem: The author claims that a judge who decides the cyclist's case on plain meaning alone:

choices.A: has applied the only standard that the legislature in fact enacted
choices.B: has arrived at the result the author regards as plainly the right one
choices.C: has consulted a purpose while denying to himself that he has done so
choices.D: relies on something unenacted and harder to contest than a stated aim

questions.explanation: The third paragraph says 'an intuition about current usage was not enacted either', and then contrasts the two unlegislated things: a stated question 'can be argued against', whereas 'a private sense of what a word covers cannot'.

wrong.A: The passage denies this, pointing out that an intuition about current usage went through no vote.
wrong.B: The author takes no view on whether a bicycle is a carriage, saying only that the word does not decide it.
wrong.C: The complaint is that such a judge consults an intuition rather than a purpose, which is why his ground cannot be argued with.

questions.stem:
The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

I. A court can identify a statute's purpose without any claim about what legislators thought
II. The suspicion that purpose has been abused by courts is unfounded
III. A judge's intuition about what a word covers is a more public standard than a stated aim

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: I and II only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Only the first is the author's view: purpose 'need not be psychological' and is 'public, textual and contestable'. The second is denied in the second paragraph, where the suspicion is called 'the right worry'. The third inverts the third paragraph, where a private sense of a word's coverage is what cannot be argued against.

wrong.B: The author says the opposite, granting that purpose 'has in fact been used as a licence for conclusions reached on other grounds'.
wrong.C: The first belongs, but the second is the very suspicion the author endorses at the outset.
wrong.D: This adds two statements the passage explicitly contradicts to the one it asserts.

questions.stem: On the author's account, a court deciding whether the lamp requirement reaches bicycles should ask:

choices.A: whether speakers today would describe a bicycle as a carriage
choices.B: what problem the requirement's own conditions show it addressed
choices.C: what the legislators who passed the bylaw would have said of bicycles
choices.D: whether any later enactment has brought bicycles within the rule

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph works the example through in exactly these terms: a requirement that applies after dark, on highways and not in private yards 'is addressed to collisions in the dark rather than to the dignity of carriages, and nothing about anyone's inner life was needed to see it'.

wrong.A: Current usage is the unenacted intuition the author objects to relying on.
wrong.C: This is the psychological conception of purpose that the author concedes to the critics and abandons.
wrong.D: A later enactment would answer a different question, and the author's problem is how to read the statute actually before the court.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that:

choices.A: planning should measure the conditions producing street life rather than its traces
choices.B: the instruments of street life agree with one another and may therefore be trusted
choices.C: the judgement of experienced planners is a better guide than any instrument
choices.D: a measure loses its usefulness the moment it is adopted as an official target

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states the recommendation: what the cases argue for is 'not less measurement but measurement aimed one step further back, at conditions rather than residues'.

wrong.B: The second paragraph begins by denying this: 'Agreement among instruments is not validation.'
wrong.C: The fifth paragraph resists exactly this conclusion, saying planning by taste 'has a worse record than planning by numbers, and it is not close'.
wrong.D: Optimisation against a target is one of two mechanisms the author names, not the conclusion of the argument.

questions.stem: The follow-up surveys of the redeveloped district found that most of its users:

choices.A: had stayed considerably longer than the counts suggested
choices.B: thought the benches and the frontage poorly designed
choices.C: had come to the district in order to meet people they knew
choices.D: had arrived by car and had visited a single destination

questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that 'most had arrived by car, had come for a single destination, stayed under forty minutes, and knew nobody else present'.

wrong.A: The reported stay was under forty minutes, and the author's point is that the counts flattered the district rather than understating it.
wrong.B: The design is described as scoring near the top of the index; no complaint about its quality is reported from users.
wrong.C: The surveys found the reverse, that users knew nobody else present.

questions.stem: In saying that agreement among the instruments is not validation, the author means that:

choices.A: the instruments were calibrated against each other rather than independently
choices.B: the association fails once density and transit access have been controlled
choices.C: measures may agree because each records a trace of the same hidden thing
choices.D: no measure of street life can be built out of observation of any kind

questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains the agreement by what the measures have in common: footfall and dwell time are 'traces left by the conditions that produce street life', and because the traces are countable and the conditions are not, 'the correlation gets read backwards'.

wrong.A: Nothing is said about how the instruments were calibrated; the objection concerns what they capture, not how they were set up.
wrong.B: The first paragraph says the association 'survives adjustment for density and transit access'.
wrong.D: The author recommends further measurement, listing countable conditions, so this overstates the position considerably.

questions.stem: The author's argument depends on each of the following claims EXCEPT that:

choices.A: planning guided by the judgement of planners has the better record
choices.B: footfall and dwell time are traces of conditions that are hard to count
choices.C: parties with money optimise for a measure once it becomes a target
choices.D: the instruments cannot record sociability that no observer witnesses

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph asserts the opposite of this: 'Planning by taste has a worse record than planning by numbers, and it is not close.' The other three are load-bearing claims from the second and fourth paragraphs.

wrong.B: This is the second paragraph's central claim and the basis of the charge that the correlation is read backwards.
wrong.C: This is the first of the two mechanisms in the fourth paragraph, illustrated by the leasing agent subdividing a frontage.
wrong.D: This is the second mechanism, which the author says a planning process disciplined by the data will steadily discount.

questions.stem: A city proposes to rate its districts by the share of ground-floor tenants holding leases of ten years or more. The author would most likely call the proposal:

choices.A: a further residue, since lease length is itself produced by street life
choices.B: unnecessary, since the existing counts already capture the same thing
choices.C: promising, though developers would capture it within a single season
choices.D: preferable, though slower and costlier to collect than a footfall count

questions.explanation: This is the author's own first example of measuring conditions rather than residues, and the paragraph immediately concedes the drawback: such measures are 'harder to collect than a pedestrian count', arrive annually, and cannot be produced by a consultant in a fortnight.

wrong.A: The author places tenure among the conditions that produce street life, not among the traces it leaves.
wrong.B: The whole argument is that the counts capture something different, which is why a district can score well and be socially empty.
wrong.C: Capture by developers is the author's worry about targets that a leasing agent can satisfy in an afternoon; a ten-year lease history is not alterable in a season.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's criticism of the standard toolkit?

choices.A: Counts are in practice taken at many more points than the passage describes
choices.B: Districts with the highest counts are where residents report most acquaintances
choices.C: Developers find the mixed-use index expensive and awkward to manipulate
choices.D: The time needed to obtain a permit varies little from one district to another

questions.explanation: The criticism is that the counts measure a residue and can rise while the thing they stand for does not, as in the waterfront district where users 'knew nobody else present'. If high counts went with dense acquaintance among residents, the proxy would be tracking what it is meant to track.

wrong.A: More observation points make the count more precise about footfall, which is not what the author doubts.
wrong.C: This blunts only the first of the two mechanisms and leaves the deeper objection, that the measure records only what a counter can see, untouched.
wrong.D: Uniform permit times would make one of the author's proposed measures less discriminating, which is an objection to the remedy rather than a defence of the toolkit.

questions.stem: The author's main contention is that:

choices.A: photographs have never been reliable evidence about anything at all
choices.B: one of the two claims made for early photography survives the correction
choices.C: the framing and timing of a photograph matter less than its development
choices.D: generated images differ from photographs only in how they are received

questions.explanation: The third paragraph sets out the structure of the argument: 'the first enthusiasm ran two claims together and the correction refutes only one of them'. The authority claim is conceded to be false; the causal claim is defended, and the last paragraph calls it 'the part worth defending'.

wrong.A: The author argues the reverse, insisting that a photograph establishes a presence even when the photographer is wholly distrusted.
wrong.C: All three are treated alike, as operations that change what a photograph shows without touching whether light came from something.
wrong.D: For generated images the author says the causal claim 'is simply unavailable', which is a difference in kind and not only in reception.

questions.stem: As the author describes it, the causal claim about a photograph is the claim that:

choices.A: the image shows how its subject was, and shows it without interpretation
choices.B: the image carries the mind of whoever composed and printed it
choices.C: the image's existence depends on something having been before the lens
choices.D: the image cannot be altered once the light has been recorded on it

questions.explanation: The third paragraph states it: 'the image was produced by light coming from the thing, so that its existence depends on the thing's having been in front of the lens'.

wrong.A: This is the second claim, about authority, which the author calls 'plainly false'.
wrong.B: Carrying a mind is what the first writers attributed to pictures made by a hand, in contrast with the photograph.
wrong.D: The author grants that development can be pushed until a grey sky turns black, so no such claim is being made.

questions.stem: The comparison between a drawing and a photograph of the same window is offered in order to:

choices.A: establish that drawings are worthless as evidence to a historian
choices.B: concede that the caption attached to a photograph can mislead
choices.C: argue that a photograph interprets its subject less than a drawing
choices.D: show that the surviving claim does work in how evidence is weighed

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by announcing this purpose: 'That the surviving claim is doing work can be seen in how evidence is actually handled.' The asymmetry is that the photographic inference 'survives distrusting the photographer entirely'.

wrong.A: The author says a drawing is evidence that the artist believed what he drew, which is a limited role rather than none.
wrong.B: A dishonest caption is granted in passing, but the comparison is there to show what remains despite such dishonesty.
wrong.C: Comparative interpretation is not the point; the author has already conceded that photographs are framed, timed and developed.

questions.stem: Suppose a photograph were taken through a lens that distorted shapes past recognition. The author would most likely say that:

choices.A: the causal claim holds, though the picture shows little of how things looked
choices.B: the picture has lost the only evidential value a photograph ever has
choices.C: the distortion counts as interpretation and therefore as authorship
choices.D: such a picture stands closer to a generated image than to a photograph

questions.explanation: Distortion belongs with framing, timing and development: operations that 'change what a photograph shows' but not 'whether light came from something'. So the causal claim is untouched and the authority claim, which the author never defends, is what suffers.

wrong.B: The evidential value the author defends is of presence rather than of appearance, and that is precisely what distortion leaves intact.
wrong.C: Authorship is granted throughout and is not in dispute; the author's claim is about what survives authorship.
wrong.D: A generated image has no causal history at all, which is the one feature this picture still has.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of generated images suggests that their arrival:

choices.A: showed by its removal how much the causal claim had been carrying
choices.B: has made the authority claim defensible again for ordinary pictures
choices.C: was welcomed by the critics who had long attacked photographic truth
choices.D: differs from earlier technical changes only in the speed of its spread

questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says 'the shape of the response to those images is itself evidence for the argument': the arrival 'was received as a loss', and even longstanding critics 'found themselves mourning something', which the author identifies as the narrower claim they had been attacking.

wrong.B: Nothing restores the authority claim, which the author calls plainly false and does not attempt to rescue.
wrong.C: The passage reports the opposite, that those critics mourned rather than welcomed the change.
wrong.D: The author stresses a difference in kind, contrasting the reception with that of colour film or the fast lens.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's argument?

choices.A: Photographers have staged scenes and captioned them dishonestly
choices.B: Early writers on photography also praised the medium for its detail
choices.C: Generated images can now be identified reliably by technical means
choices.D: Viewers treat a photograph as evidence of presence only if they trust its maker

questions.explanation: The argument's load-bearing observation is the asymmetry in the fourth paragraph: the photographic inference 'survives distrusting the photographer entirely'. If the inference actually depended on trusting the maker, photographs would be in the same position as drawings and the surviving claim would do no work.

wrong.A: This is among the observations the author accepts in the second paragraph and argues to be compatible with the causal claim.
wrong.B: Praise for detail is simply a further remark about what early writers admired and bears on neither of the two claims.
wrong.C: Reliable detection would help preserve the distinction the author draws rather than undermine it.

questions.stem: The household studies described in the passage found that a dish is policed most firmly where:

choices.A: the story of the dish's ancestry is thinnest
choices.B: the cooks do not know the dish is recent
choices.C: a restaurant guide has certified the dish
choices.D: a state agency has promoted it for export

questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that dishes 'are maintained most carefully, and deviation policed most firmly, in precisely the cases where the ancestry story is thinnest'.

wrong.B: The studies describe cooks who know the history and will say so cheerfully, which is what makes the finding interesting.
wrong.C: Certification appears later as one way the authority can be captured, not as a condition found in the household studies.
wrong.D: Export campaigns belong to the first paragraph's account of how dishes became canonical, not to these findings.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.A: the historical research on national cuisines has been largely mistaken
choices.B: claims of authenticity are marketing campaigns that cooks have absorbed
choices.C: a dish is authentic when those who cook it agree about its ancestry
choices.D: authenticity is a claim about authority within a practice, not about descent

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states it: what cooks assert is 'a claim about a practice: that there is a right way to do this, that the standard is held by the people who cook it', so that 'authenticity in this sense is a question of authority, not of origin'.

wrong.A: The author calls the history right and the final paragraph calls it indispensable; the objection is to an inference drawn from it.
wrong.B: This is the debunking conclusion the passage criticises as too quick.
wrong.C: Agreement about ancestry is what the author argues is not at issue, since cooks who concede the history keep the standard.

questions.stem: The author says the debunking conclusion has the same defect as the myth it corrects. That defect is that it:

choices.A: rests on evidence too thin to support a claim so broad
choices.B: does not attend to what the people it describes are doing
choices.C: assumes that a cuisine must have a single place of origin
choices.D: treats cooks as the authorities on their own practice

questions.explanation: The second paragraph names the defect in these words: 'it does not attend to what the people it describes are actually doing'.

wrong.A: The author grants the historical evidence and calls the pattern it establishes almost tiringly regular.
wrong.C: Origins are the debunkers' subject but the passage does not accuse them of assuming a single one.
wrong.D: This is the author's own position, arrived at in the fourth paragraph, rather than a defect charged against anyone.

questions.stem:
The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

I. A cook who learns that a dish is recent has reason to relax its standards
II. An account of authenticity should explain why the historical findings persuade so few
III. The risk that authenticity will be captured is a defect in the author's own account

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: II and III only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Only the second is the author's view, and the fourth paragraph counts it as a merit of the account that it 'explains the one feature of the debate that the debunkers never explain, which is that their findings persuade nobody'. The first is denied in the same paragraph, and the third in the fifth, where the risk is 'a risk of the practice rather than of the description'.

wrong.A: The author says such a cook 'has been told nothing that bears on whether the method is being done properly'.
wrong.C: The second belongs, but the third is explicitly refused: the capture risk is said not to be an objection to the account.
wrong.D: This adds both statements the passage denies to the one it endorses.

questions.stem: A cook tells a researcher that her family learned the dish from a magazine in the 1950s and that a neighbour who alters the method is doing it wrong. The author would most likely treat this as:

choices.A: a confusion that the historical research is designed to clear up
choices.B: evidence that the claim of authenticity concerns descent after all
