choices.C: an ordinary instance of the practice-based claim the passage describes
choices.D: a sign that the dish has been captured by a nationalist campaign

questions.explanation: This is the household pattern the third paragraph reports and the fourth explains: cooks who concede the recent history 'still treat a change in method as a fault to be corrected', because the claim is about the right way to do it rather than about ancestry.

wrong.A: The author insists such cooks 'are not confused', since conceding the history leaves their standard untouched.
wrong.B: The cook has conceded the descent story, which is why the case tells against the descent reading rather than for it.
wrong.D: Capture involves guides and campaigns speaking for a practice, and nothing of the kind appears in a household correcting a neighbour.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most WEAKEN the author's position?

choices.A: Several canonical dishes prove to be older than the research had suggested
choices.B: Restaurant guides increasingly certify dishes against a written recipe
choices.C: Cooks shown that a dish is recent generally stop correcting deviations
choices.D: Migrant households alter their dishes as the local ingredients require

questions.explanation: The argument rests on the observation that conceding the history leaves the standard in place: 'If the claim to authenticity were a historical claim about descent, people who had conceded the history would have abandoned the claim. They do not.' A finding that they do abandon it removes the only evidence for the practice-based reading.

wrong.A: The author's account is indifferent to a dish's age, and is offered partly to explain why cooks of old and new dishes are equally firm.
wrong.B: Certification is the capture the author anticipates, and he treats it as a risk of the practice rather than a difficulty for the account.
wrong.D: Changes made for a reason acceptable to practitioners are permitted by the account, which requires a reason rather than stasis.

questions.stem: The passage argues chiefly that:

choices.A: games provide a rest from the constraints that work imposes
choices.B: a game's value lies in difficulties accepted for their own sake
choices.C: professional sport has destroyed the games that it took over
choices.D: games are best understood as works of art of a minor kind

questions.explanation: The first paragraph states the thesis, that a player 'accepts a thicket of rules nobody obliged him to accept ... in order to make something difficult that was not difficult before', and the last calls games 'the clearest available case of a seriousness with no purpose beyond itself'.

wrong.A: This is the account the passage opens by rejecting, saying 'almost everything about this is backwards'.
wrong.C: The author claims professionalisation corrodes a sport and names the mechanisms, which is weaker than destruction and is one case rather than the thesis.
wrong.D: The fifth paragraph limits the comparison with art, noting that a game leaves no product and that a theory treating games as artworks looks for something that was never there.

questions.stem: The chess player who wins because his opponent's hand slipped is introduced in order to show that:

choices.A: what the player wanted was the difficulty and not the result
choices.B: the rules of chess are too strict to allow for a fair outcome
choices.C: players are unreliable judges of why they have won a game
choices.D: winning matters more during a game than it does afterwards

questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the player 'has the result he was playing for and feels cheated, and he feels cheated of the only thing that was actually at stake, which was the difficulty'.

wrong.B: The slip is the opponent's accident rather than a consequence of the rules, and the author nowhere criticises chess for strictness.
wrong.C: The player's sense of having been cheated is treated as accurate and is the evidence the author relies on.
wrong.D: That observation is made in the preceding sentence about winning and twenty minutes afterwards; the chess example is brought in to make the sharper point.

questions.stem: The author's account of games would be supported by all of the following observations EXCEPT:

choices.A: A golfer declines the offer of an implement better suited to the task
choices.B: Players abandon a game whose obstacles have grown too easy to matter
choices.C: Spectators lose interest in a sport once its prize money declines
choices.D: A runner chooses a longer route in order to make the run harder

questions.explanation: Interest that tracks prize money is interest in a value 'whose value now comes from outside', which is what the author says corrodes a game. The other three are cases of difficulty sought for its own sake, which is the thesis of the first two paragraphs.

wrong.A: This is the author's own example, since the golfer has agreed to use 'the least suitable implements he could find'.
wrong.B: If the obstacle is the activity, a game that has become easy has lost what players came for, exactly as the account predicts.
wrong.D: Choosing an unnecessary difficulty is the behaviour the account was devised to explain.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of professional sport is best described as:

choices.A: a concession that weakens the account he has given
choices.B: an illustration chosen because it raises no difficulty
choices.C: a hard case that the account turns out to explain
choices.D: evidence that games ought not to be played for money

questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph introduces it as 'the hard case for this account' and then reports that what the account predicts is 'what happens': deliberate fouls and time-wasting, made rationally once the outcome's value comes from outside.

wrong.A: The author draws the opposite conclusion, treating the corrosion of professional sport as confirmation rather than as a cost.
wrong.B: The passage calls it hard precisely because winning there has consequences outside the game.
wrong.D: No recommendation about money is offered; the paragraph explains a change in what the activity is.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most WEAKEN the author's argument?

choices.A: Players who remove a game's hardest rules report enjoying it more
choices.B: Some poets write in forms stricter than any their subject requires
choices.C: Deliberate fouls are punished by a fine in most professional leagues
choices.D: Most people describe their games as a relief from the working day

questions.explanation: The thesis is that the obstacle is the activity and that to remove it is to 'dissolve the problem' rather than to liberate anything. If players consistently enjoyed a game more once its hardest constraints were stripped out, the obstacle would be a cost they tolerate rather than the thing they came for.

wrong.B: This supports the author, since a form stricter than the subject requires is difficulty manufactured for its own sake.
wrong.C: How a league penalises fouling says nothing about why a player reckons the foul worth making.
wrong.D: The passage addresses this description at the outset and argues that the behaviour of players tells against it, so repeating it adds no new evidence.
